Zubin stood outside the lecture hall at nineteen and counted the ways he did not belong. Everyone had come from famous schools. His marks were ordinary, he thought, and the admission was luck. When his friend Nirmala said, "You always explain things so well," he laughed it off. "I just got lucky with that topic." He compared his notes to hers and only saw what was missing.
At twenty-two, Zubin joined a small company as an intern. On Friday his manager Nikita called him over. "Good work," Nikita said, and Zubin nodded while his mind filed it under politeness. Then Nikita opened his report on the screen. "Your summary put the three customer complaints in order of cost, and that let the team fix the biggest one first. That was your decision, and it saved a week." Zubin looked at the page. It was his own list. He could not wave that away as easily as a friendly comment. He wrote the sentence in his notebook and kept it open on his desk that weekend.

qa.q: How did Zubin reply when Nirmala said he always explained things so well?
qa.a: He laughed it off and said, "I just got lucky with that topic."

qa.q: Why did Nikita's feedback reach Zubin when a kinder-sounding remark did not?
qa.a: Zubin's habit at nineteen was to wave off praise as luck or politeness. Nikita's comment named exactly what he did, the ordering of complaints by cost, so it gave his doubting mind something concrete to accept.

qa.q: What was Zubin thinking when he nodded at Nikita's first "Good work"?
qa.a: He was probably doubtful and guarded, treating it as politeness rather than proof, because he did not yet believe he had earned it.

qa.q: How could Nirmala give Zubin better encouragement at college?
qa.a: Nirmala could name a particular thing, such as how he broke the topic into steps, so that her praise is specific and harder for him to dismiss.

grounding: A student who feels like a fraud (4092) is later given specific, honest praise by a manager that his doubting mind can accept (3228).
